==English==

===Pronunciation===
* {{enPR|frē}}, {{IPA|en|/fɹiː/|[fɹɪi̯]|a=RP}}
* {{audio|en|En-uk-free.ogg|a=RP}}
* {{IPA|en|/fɹɪj/|a=SSB}}
* {{IPA|en|/fɹi/|a=GA}}
* {{audio|en|En-us-free.ogg|a=GA}}
* {{homophones|en|three|aa=th-fronting}}
* {{rhymes|en|iː|s=1}}

===Etymology 1===
{{etymon|en|id=adjective|:inh|enm:fre|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|fre}}, from {{inh|en|ang|frēo}}, {{m|ang|frēoh}}, {{m|ang|frī}}, {{m|ang|friġ}}, {{m|ang|frīoh|t=free}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*frī}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*frijaz|t=beloved, not in bondage}}, from {{inh|en|ine-pro|*priHós|t=pleased, loved}}, from {{m|ine-pro|*preyH-|t=to please; to love}}. Related to {{m|en|friend}}.
{{box-top|cognates, etc}}
Germanic cognates include {{cog|sco|fre|t=free}}, {{cog|frr|frai}}, {{m|frr|frei}}, {{m|frr|fri}}, {{m|frr|Frii|t=free}}, {{cog|stq|fräi|t=free}}, {{cog|fy|frij|t=free}}, {{cog|nl|vrij|t=free}}, {{cog|de|frei|t=free}}, {{cog|nds|free|t=free}}, {{cog|lb|fräi|t=free}}, {{cog|wym|frȧj|t=free}}, {{cog|yi|פֿרײַ|t=free}}, {{cog|da,nb,nn,sv|fri|t=free}}, {{cog|fo|fríur|t=free}}, {{cog|got|𐍆𐍂𐌴𐌹𐍃|t=free}}.

Other cognates include {{cog|kw|rydh|t=free}}, {{cog|cy|rhydd|t=free}}, {{cog|la|propriō|t=to appropriate}}, {{cog|cs|přát|t=to wish; to favour}}, {{cog|pl|sprzyjać|t=to favour, foster}}, {{cog|sh|прѝјати}}, {{m|sh|prìjati|t=to please, taste, suit; to be agreeable, relish}}, {{cog|sk|priať|t=to wish}}, {{cog|ae|𐬟𐬭𐬌𐬌𐬀|t=good, pleasant}}, {{cog|fa|فری|tr=fari|t=beloved, dear; agreeable, pleasing}}, {{cog|sa|प्रिय|t=beloved}}.

Germanic and Celtic are the only Indo-European language branches in which the PIE word with the meaning of "dear, beloved" acquired the additional meaning of "free" in the sense of "not in bondage". This was an extension of the idea of "characteristic of those who are dear and beloved", in other words friends and tribe members (in contrast to unfree inhabitants from other tribes and prisoners of war, many of which were among the slaves – compare the Latin use of [[liberi]] to mean both "free persons" and "children of a family").<ref>{{R:Etymonline}}</ref><ref>[https://www.dwds.de/wb/frei "frei"] in Digitales Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache</ref>
{{box-bottom}}

|passage=There was some laughter, and Roddle was left '''free''' to expand his ideas on the periodic visits of cowboys to the town. “Mason Rickets, he had ten big punkins a-sittin' in front of his store, an' them fellers from the Upside-down-F ranch shot 'em up {{...}}.”}}

|passage=Policing the relationship between government and business in a '''free''' society is difficult. Businesspeople have every right to lobby governments, and civil servants to take jobs in the private sector.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20170702024409/http://www.economist.com/news/business/21583242-businesspeople-have-become-too-influential-government-cronies-and-capitols|archivedate=2 July 2017}}

## {{senseid|en|algebraically generic or universal}} {{lb|en|algebra|of an [[algebraic structure]]}} {{non-gloss|In any of various technical senses}} [[generic]], [[universal]].
### {{lb|en|category theory|of a functor <math>F</math>}} Left [[adjoint]] to a [[forgetful functor]] <math>G</math>; such that any map <math>f : X \to G(A)</math> induces a universal map <math>\bar f : F(X)\to A</math>.
### {{lb|en|category theory|of an object}} Belonging to the [[image]] of some free functor.
### {{lb|en|group theory|of a group}} Having a set of [[generators]] which satisfy no [[non-trivial]] [[relation]]s; equivalently, being the group of [[reduced word]]s on a set of generators.
###: {{ux|en|The [[fundamental group]] of the [[figure eight]] is '''free''' of rank 2.}}
### {{lb|en|[[commutative algebra]]|of a [[module]]}} Having a [[linearly independent]] set of generators (called a [[basis]]).

##: {{ant|en|bound}}

But even here I was not '''free''' from interruption, for he was seated on a horse-block below me, playing with a fox terrier.}}
